Abstract The adaptive immune system and neurodegenerative Alzheimer's disease (AD) are intertwined in multiple ways. Recent studies have reported alterations of the adaptive immune system in early AD stages, such as preclinical AD and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) due to AD. However, the identity of specific antigenic targets and whether the respective response is beneficial or detrimental during disease progression are still open questions. Herein, we describe cross-sectional analyses of blood and CSF from three different study populations covering early AD stages. We employed high-dimensional mass cytometry, single-cell RNA-sequencing, ex vivo T-cell secretome analysis, and antigen presentation assays to achieve a comprehensive characterization of adaptive immune cell populations. Our results show that subjects at the stage of asymptomatic, preclinical AD can mount a CD4 + T helper cell response towards amyloid-β peptide and display an early enrichment of CD8 + T effector memory cells re-expressing CD45RA (TEMRA cells) in CSF, combined with a less immunosuppressive gene signature of peripheral regulatory T cells. Conversely, in MCI we observed increased frequencies of CD8 + TEMRA/effector cells in the periphery characterized by a pro-inflammatory gene expression profile, and generally decreased antigen responsiveness. Our results demonstrate the complexity of adaptive immune changes in early AD and suggest that it may be beneficial to promote specific CD4 + T-cell responses in the preclinical stage, while in MCI it may be important to therapeutically target CD8 + T-cell responses if these prove to be harmful. Rickenbach et al. explore how the adaptive immune system changes in early Alzheimer's disease. They show that during the preclinical phase, a CD4+ T-cell response to amyloid-β epitopes emerges. In individuals with biomarker-positive mild cognitive impairment, however, there are signs of potentially harmful T-cell activity. See Skelly et al. Introduction Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disease affecting over 50 million people worldwide. 1 Hallmarks of AD pathology are aggregation and deposition of misfolded amyloid-β peptide (Aβ) into Aβ plaques, neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau, and neurodegeneration. 2 After a long asymptomatic preclinical phase with Aβ accumulation followed by tau pathology, AD can progress along a continuum to mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia. 3-7 Biomarkers for AD, including cerebral Aβ and tau aggregates measured by PET scans, along with elevated levels of phosphorylated tau species (p-tau) in CSF or plasma, can predict the probability of a clinical transition from cognitively healthy individuals to MCI and dementia. 8-10 Importantly, preclinical AD refers to cognitively normal individuals with increased risk, rather than a certainty of progression to MCI or AD, as many biomarker-positive, cognitively unimpaired individuals remain stable for extended periods while others do progress. 11 As particularly the preclinical phase of AD is not well understood, its in-depth characterization would allow improving biomarkers and potentially preventive therapeutic strategies before the onset of symptoms. In recent years, the role of adaptive immunity in AD has been increasingly recognized. Both clinical and genetic data suggest an involvement of inflammation-related pathways in AD pathogenesis and progression. 12 , 13 Multiple studies have identified increased T-cell infiltration in AD brains, 14-16 sparking the question of whether the underlying responses might be beneficial or detrimental during disease progression. For the CD8 + subtype of T cells, T effector memory cells re-expressing CD45RA (TEMRA) were shown to be increased in peripheral blood and CSF of AD patients. 14 Interestingly, immunophenotyping studies focusing on earlier stages of AD revealed that CD8 + TEMRA cells are altered even before the conversion to AD dementia 17 as early as in preclinical AD. 18 While lymphocyte infiltration in AD brains appears to be a targeted process, the antigenic target remains unknown. 19 Some studies investigated the T-cell antigen specificity in AD and reported reactivity of CD4 + T cells towards Aβ-derived epitopes in a human leucocyte antigen (HLA) class II-dependent manner. 20-22 These results were no surprise as earlier studies observed that immunization with Aβ peptide resulted in less AD pathology in mouse models of β-amyloidosis. 23 The subsequent first active immunization strategy for AD was AN-1792, mainly consisting of synthetic full-length Aβ 1-42 peptide. Clinical trials were suspended due to cases of meningoencephalitis. 24 Nevertheless, T-cell recruitment to the CNS occurred, and some responders mounted antibody responses against the amino-terminus (N-terminus) of Aβ. 25 Further discoveries of human autoantibodies directed against aggregated Aβ support the concept of successful priming of the adaptive immune system in AD. 26-28 To investigate the onset, targets and nature of AD-associated T-cell responses, we performed an in-depth cross-sectional immunophenotyping of three study populations covering the early stages of AD. We included cognitively healthy subjects with early evidence of cerebral β-amyloidosis (referred to as preclinical AD) and subjects with MCI due to AD (also referred to as prodromal AD). We provide a detailed analysis of immune cell populations in peripheral blood and CSF by combining mass cytometry by time-of-flight (CyTOF) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq). Additionally, we performed a functional analysis of the T-cell secretome and antigen presentation assays. We report that CD4 + T cells in preclinical AD display a type 2 T-helper profile and reactivity against carboxyl-terminal (C-terminal) and mid-sequence peptides derived from linear Aβ 1-42 . In contrast, we observe an increased frequency and a more pro-inflammatory gene expression of CD8 + TEMRA/effector cells in MCI subjects. Our analysis suggests a potentially beneficial role for activated CD4 + T helper cells in preclinical AD and a potentially harmful involvement of CD8 + T cells when the pathology becomes clinically symptomatic.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Adaptive immune changes across the early Alzheimer's disease continuum, including preclinical AD and mild cognitive impairment (MCI), focusing on immunophenotype and function of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the context of Aβ and tau pathology.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Adaptive immune responses are functionally distinct across early AD stages. In preclinical AD, CD4+ T helper cells exhibit a less pro-inflammatory, more TH2-like phenotype, secrete B cell-stimulating cytokines (IL-4), and react specifically against Aβ mid-sequence and C-terminus epitopes, suggesting a potentially protective response. CD8+ TEMRA/effector cells are enriched in CSF, showing a less pro-inflammatory gene signature. Peripheral regulatory T cells (Tregs) show a less immunosuppressive gene signature, potentially allowing for these adaptive responses. Conversely, in Aβ-positive MCI, CD8+ TEMRA/effector cells increase in frequency in the periphery, display a pro-inflammatory gene expression profile, and their expansion is linked to neurodegeneration and tau pathology, potentially driving neuronal loss. Tregs remain less immunosuppressive. A general decrease in antigen responsiveness, including to Aβ epitopes, is observed in MCI, possibly due to exhaustion or impaired antigen presentation. Immune tolerance mechanisms suppress T-cell responses to the Aβ N-terminus, creating an epitope mismatch where beneficial responses target less accessible Aβ regions. This combined immunological shift contributes to a hyper-inflammatory environment in MCI and AD.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The study compared adaptive immune responses across the early AD continuum, categorizing individuals by Aβ status (Aβ-negative HCS, Aβ-positive HCS, Aβ-positive MCI) based on CSF Aβ42/40 ratio or cerebral Aβ PET load (FMM Centiloid >12). It observed distinct T-cell profiles and reactivity shifts with disease progression. CD8+ TEMRA/effector cells showed a less pro-inflammatory signature in preclinical AD, which reversed to more pro-inflammatory in Aβ-positive MCI, with increased abundance in MCI subjects with elevated p-tau181/p-tau217. CD4+ memory T-cell reactivity to AD-related antigens was increased in cognitively healthy subjects but generally decreased in MCI, with lower frequencies of IL-4 and IL-13 producing T helper cell subsets in Aβ-positive MCI. These findings highlight progression-related changes rather than specific dose-response relationships.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: CD4+ T helper cell responses are specifically directed towards amyloid-β peptide, particularly mid-sequence and C-terminal fragments of Aβ 1-42, but not the N-terminus, likely due to peripheral tolerance. This antigen-specific response is intact in cognitively healthy (preclinical AD) subjects but diminishes in Aβ-positive MCI, indicating a change in specificity with disease progression. The expansion of CD8+ TEMRA/effector cells in early AD stages was found to be independent of latent Herpesviridae infections. The study acknowledges that its stringent selection of linear, high-HLA-affinity tau peptides might have overlooked some tau-specific immune responses, especially those involving post-translational modifications.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: The study targets individuals across the early Alzheimer's disease continuum, including cognitively healthy controls (HCS), individuals in the asymptomatic preclinical AD stage (Aβ-positive HCS), and those with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), specifically Aβ-positive MCI (MCI+) and p-tau217 positive MCI subjects.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Adaptive immune changes in early AD are complex and functionally distinct. In preclinical AD, a less immunosuppressive Treg profile and a T H 2-like CD4+ T-cell response to Aβ-derived epitopes suggest a potentially protective adaptive immune response. Conversely, in MCI, increased frequencies of pro-inflammatory CD8+ TEMRA/effector cells and continued less immunosuppressive Tregs contribute to a hyper-inflammatory environment, associated with neurodegeneration, plasma NfL elevation, hippocampal atrophy, and cognitive decline. T-cell hypo-responsiveness and impaired antigen presentation in MCI may hinder Aβ clearance. These findings highlight the need for tailored immunomodulatory therapies: promoting beneficial CD4+ T-cell responses in the preclinical stage and potentially targeting harmful CD8+ T-cell responses in MCI to mitigate neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: In preclinical AD, the immune profile, characterized by activated CD4+ T helper cells responding to Aβ, suggests a potential protective benefit. Conversely, increased CD8+ TEMRA/effector cells and a less immunosuppressive Treg signature in MCI are associated with adverse risks, contributing to a hyper-inflammatory environment, neurodegeneration, and cognitive decline. T-cell hypo-responsiveness and impaired phagocyte function in Aβ-positive MCI pose an adverse risk by potentially reducing Aβ clearance. The elevation of CD8+ TEMRA/effector cells in early AD stages, including preclinical AD and MCI, indicates diagnostic/prognostic utility. Interventions like immune checkpoint blockade or enhancing Tregs are considered to offer protective benefits by reducing pathology and mitigating neuroinflammation, whereas broad immunosuppressive strategies carry treatment risks by potentially inhibiting both harmful and protective pathways.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The study utilized robust and state-of-the-art methodologies including high-dimensional mass cytometry, single-cell RNA-sequencing, ex vivo T-cell secretome analysis, and antigen presentation assays for comprehensive immune cell characterization. The increase of CD8+ TEMRA/effector cells in early AD stages (MCI+ and p-tau positive individuals) was confirmed, replicated, and found to be independent of latent Herpesviridae infections, bolstering the reliability of this finding. Age and sex had minor influences on T-cell abundances. The study acknowledged that previous Aβ reactivity studies lacked detailed AD biomarker analysis, and its own stringent selection criteria for tau peptides might have missed certain tau-specific immune responses, highlighting limitations in antigen candidate pools.
